definition: The song itself, music plus any lyrics, separate from any recording of it. Usually held by the songwriter or a publisher.
One fixed performance of a song. A separate copyright from the composition, usually held by a label or the artist.
Re-performing part of an existing song instead of lifting the recording. It uses the composition only, so it needs publishing clearance and no master license.
Permission from the owner of the sound recording.
Permission from the owner of the composition.
The US section 115 license to make and distribute recordings of a musical work, the route used for cover versions. Sample clearance has no equivalent and is a free negotiation.
A taking so small the law ignores it. In the Ninth Circuit, one an average audience would not recognize.
Two US federal appeals courts giving opposite answers to the same question. On sampling, the two are Bridgeport (Sixth Circuit, 2005) and VMG Salsoul (Ninth Circuit, 2016).
A US defense that weighs four factors case by case. It contains no fixed number of seconds or notes.
A use that gives the borrowed material a new purpose or message. Central to fair use since Campbell (1994); the Supreme Court revisited it in Warhol (2023).
Exact copying of a small part of a work, as in sampling. The question becomes whether the part taken matters.
The UK infringement test: whether an important part of the work was taken, judged by quality as much as quantity.
The UK's exceptions for listed purposes such as caricature, parody and pastiche. It asks whether more was taken than needed and whether the use competes with the original.
In EU law since the 2026 Pelham II ruling: a creation that evokes an existing work, is noticeably different from it, and engages with it in an objectively recognizable creative dialogue.
The EU and Japanese legal term for whoever first fixes a recording, usually the label. Holds a right of its own in the recording.
Rights of performers and record producers that sit next to the author's copyright.
Personal rights to be credited and to object to distortion of a work or performance. Japan gives them to performers.
US recordings made before February 15, 1972, which had no federal protection until the Music Modernization Act of 2018.
The idea that the limitation clock starts when the owner learns of the infringement. The Supreme Court assumed it without deciding in Warner Chappell v. Nealy (2024).
The sheet music lodged with the US Copyright Office. For songs under the 1909 Act it defines what the copyright covers.
